## Intuition

The method of **Lagrange multipliers** finds the local maxima and minima of a
function (such as profit or cost) subject to equality constraints (such as a
budget or physical limit). The key idea is that at an optimum the contour
lines of the objective are tangent to the constraint surface, so the gradient
of the objective is a scalar multiple of the gradient of the constraint.

The method converts a constrained problem into one to which the derivative
test of an unconstrained problem can be applied, through the **Lagrangian**.
It is generalised to inequality constraints by the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker
conditions (see [[optimization]]).

## The Lagrangian

:::{.definition data-title="Lagrangian"}

For an objective $f$ and constraint function $g$ the **Lagrangian** is
$$
\mathcal{L}(x,\lambda):= f(x)+\left< \lambda,g(x) \right>,
$$
where $\left< \cdot,\cdot \right>$ is the [[inner-product-space|inner
product]]. The vector $\lambda$ is the **Lagrange multiplier**.

:::

To optimise $f$ subject to $g(x)=0$ we find the stationary points of
$\mathcal{L}$ in $(x,\lambda)$,
$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x}=0\quad \& \quad
\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial \lambda} = 0,
$$
or equivalently
$$
\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x} + \lambda \cdot \frac{\partial g(x)}{\partial x}=0
\quad \& \quad g(x)=0.
$$
The solution of the constrained problem is a saddle point of the Lagrangian,
which can be identified among the stationary points by the definiteness of the
bordered Hessian (see [[jacobian-and-hessian]]). The mechanics Lagrangian
$K-U$ is a different object, see [[lagrangian-mechanics]].

## Lagrange Multiplier Theorem

:::{.theorem data-title="Lagrange Multiplier Theorem"}

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and $g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^c$ be $C^1$
(continuous first derivatives). Let $\boldsymbol{x}_{\star}$ maximise
$f(\boldsymbol{x})$ subject to $g(\boldsymbol{x})=0$, and suppose the matrix
of partial derivatives
$$
\left[ \mathrm{D} g(\boldsymbol{x}_{\star}) \right] _{j,k}=
\frac{\partial g_{j}}{\partial x_{k}}
$$
has $\mathrm{rank}(\mathrm{D}g(\boldsymbol{x}_{\star}))= c \leq n$. Then there
exists a unique **Lagrange multiplier** $\lambda_{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^c$ with
$$
\mathrm{D}f(\boldsymbol{x}_{\star})=
\lambda_{\star}^{\top}\mathrm{D}g(\boldsymbol{x}_{\star}).
$$

:::

In words: at a constrained local extremum, if the constraint qualification
(the rank condition) holds, the gradient of the objective is a linear
combination of the gradients of the constraints, with the multipliers as
coefficients. Equivalently, the directional derivative of $f$ is zero in every
feasible direction: any direction perpendicular to all constraint gradients is
also perpendicular to $\nabla f$.

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="Box Volume"}

Find the box of largest volume with total surface area $64\,\mathrm{cm}^2$.
With side lengths $a,b,c>0$ we maximise $f(a,b,c)=abc$ subject to
$g(a,b,c)=ab+bc+ac-32=0$. The system is
$$
\begin{cases}
\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g:\quad
\begin{pmatrix} bc \\ ac \\ ab \end{pmatrix} =
\lambda \begin{pmatrix} b+c \\ a+c \\ a+b \end{pmatrix}, \\[1ex]
g(a,b,c) = 0.
\end{cases}
$$
Multiplying the components of the first equation by $a,b,c$ respectively gives
$abc=\lambda a(b+c)=\lambda b(a+c)=\lambda c(a+b)$. Since $abc\neq0$ we have
$\lambda\neq0$, so $ab+ac=ab+bc=ac+bc$, which forces $a=b=c$. The constraint
then gives $3a^2=32$, so $a=b=c=\sqrt{32/3}$: a cube, as expected.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Multiple Constraints"}

Find the extrema of $f(x,y,z)=4y-2z$ subject to $g_{1}=2x-y-z-2=0$ and
$g_{2}=x^2+y^2-1=0$. With two constraints there are two multipliers, and
$$
\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 4 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} =
\lambda_{1}\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}
+\lambda_{2}\begin{pmatrix} 2x \\ 2y \\ 0 \end{pmatrix},\quad g_{1}=0,\quad g_{2}=0.
$$
The third component gives $\lambda_{1}=2$. The first two then give
$x\lambda_{2}=-2$ and $y\lambda_{2}=3$, and $g_{2}=0$ yields
$\lambda_{2}=\pm\sqrt{13}$. For $\lambda_{2}=+\sqrt{13}$,
$$
(x,y,z)=\left(-\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}},\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}},
-2-\tfrac{7}{\sqrt{13}}\right),
$$
and for $\lambda_{2}=-\sqrt{13}$,
$$
(x,y,z)=\left(\tfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}},-\tfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}},
-2+\tfrac{7}{\sqrt{13}}\right).
$$
Evaluating $f$ at the two points identifies the maximum and the minimum.

:::
